title: What $1 Million Actually Buys You in 2027

scenes.text: Hi, I'm Ryan Rover. One million dollars. For a hundred years it's been the number. The word millionaire still means rich to most people. But here's a question almost nobody asks. What does one million dollars actually buy you, in real life, in twenty twenty seven? Because the answer is very different from what most people imagine.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Everyone wants a million dollars. Almost nobody knows what it buys.

scenes.text: One million dollars. Seven figures. The number on the lottery ticket, the number in the movies. Today we're going to take it apart, and see what's really inside.

Some people think a million dollars means never working again, a mansion, and a sports car. Others think it's not much money anymore. The truth sits in between, and it depends on three things: how you hold the money, where you live, and how you spend. Get those right, and a million dollars can buy you something more valuable than any car. Get them wrong, and it can disappear in a few years.
scenes.caption: MANSION AND SPORTS CAR?

scenes.text: So we'll look at it from three angles. First, the numbers: what a million is worth after inflation, taxes and fees. Then the psychology: why a million feels so different from what people expect. And finally the playbook: how to make a million dollars actually work for you. Along the way, fifteen hard truths about seven figures.
scenes.caption: 3 ANGLES, 15 TRUTHS

scenes.text: Let's start with a quick word on where the numbers come from.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Inflation figures come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer price index. Household spending comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Expenditure Survey. Home prices come from the National Association of Realtors. Social Security amounts come from the Social Security Administration, and health insurance costs from KFF's employer health benefits survey.
scenes.caption: OUR SOURCES

scenes.text: Whenever we show growth, we use a seven percent average yearly return as an illustration. Withdrawal examples use the well known four percent rule of thumb, which is a starting point, not a guarantee. This video is education, not financial advice. Your taxes, your health and your city all change the math.
scenes.query: Calculator and pen on financial papers
scenes.caption: EDUCATION, NOT ADVICE

scenes.text: Angle one. The numbers. Let's put one million dollars on the table and see what it really turns into.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: The most common way to think about it is the four percent rule of thumb. Withdraw four percent in the first year, then adjust for inflation. On one million dollars, that's about forty thousand dollars a year, before taxes.

card.note: Rule of thumb from Bengen (1994). Not a guarantee.

scenes.text: Forty thousand dollars a year. Let that sink in. That's a real income, and you never have to go to work for it. But it's also far less than most people imagine when they think of a millionaire. It's roughly what a full time job paying about twenty dollars an hour earns. Comfortable in many places. Not a mansion, not a yacht.
scenes.caption: ABOUT $40,000 A YEAR

scenes.text: Now compare that with what Americans actually spend. The Bureau of Labor Statistics found the average household spent about seventy seven thousand dollars in twenty twenty three. At that spending, one million dollars covers about thirteen years if it earned nothing at all.

card.note: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Expenditure Survey 2023

scenes.text: Of course, a million dollars that's invested doesn't sit still. That's the whole point. But this comparison shows why a million isn't the endless pile of money it sounds like. Spend like the average household, and you'd need closer to two million dollars invested to support that lifestyle with the four percent rule. That's why your spending is just as important as your balance.
scenes.caption: SPENDING DECIDES

scenes.text: And here's a number that surprises people. In Charles Schwab's Modern Wealth Survey from twenty twenty four, Americans said it takes about two and a half million dollars to be considered wealthy. So by the public's own definition, a millionaire isn't wealthy anymore. A million dollars has quietly moved from rich to comfortable.
scenes.caption: RICH OR COMFORTABLE?

scenes.text: So now let's go through the fifteen hard truths about one million dollars. Some will surprise you, a few might annoy you, and one or two could change the way you plan your whole financial life. Let's start with the one nobody puts in the movies.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Truth number one. Inflation has already cut the million dollars in half.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 1

scenes.text: According to the consumer price index from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, prices have roughly doubled since the mid nineteen nineties. That means one million dollars today buys about what five hundred thousand dollars bought back then. When your parents dreamed of being millionaires, they were dreaming of something worth twice as much as today's million.
scenes.caption: PRICES DOUBLED

scenes.text: And inflation doesn't stop. At an average of three percent a year, prices double again in about twenty four years. So if you're thirty today and you reach one million at fifty five, that million might buy what about five hundred thousand buys now. Try this: when you set a money goal for the far future, think in today's dollars. It keeps you honest about what you'll really need.
scenes.caption: THINK IN TODAY'S DOLLARS

scenes.text: Truth number two. As an income, a million dollars is about forty thousand dollars a year.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 2

scenes.text: This comes from research by financial planner William Bengen, published in nineteen ninety four. He looked at historical market returns and found that withdrawing about four percent in the first year, then adjusting for inflation, lasted at least thirty years in every period he studied. It became famous as the four percent rule.
scenes.caption: $1M = ~$40K A YEAR

scenes.text: But it's a rule of thumb, not a law. If you retire right before a big crash, or if inflation runs hot, the math gets tighter. And if you retire young, your money needs to last fifty years, not thirty, so many planners suggest something closer to three or three and a half percent. At three and a half percent, one million dollars supports about thirty five thousand dollars a year.
scenes.caption: NOT A LAW

scenes.text: Truth number three. You could buy about two and a half typical homes, and then you'd have nothing to live on.

card.title: A house, and then nothing
card.sub: two and a half median homes

scenes.caption: TRUTH 3

scenes.text: The National Association of Realtors reports the median price of an existing home sold in the United States was a little over four hundred thousand dollars in twenty twenty five. So a million dollars could buy two typical homes outright, with change left over. Sounds amazing. But a house doesn't pay your grocery bill. It costs money every year: taxes, insurance, repairs.
scenes.caption: ~$400K MEDIAN HOME

scenes.text: Here's the trap. Put six hundred thousand into a house, and you have four hundred thousand left invested. At the four percent rule, that's sixteen thousand dollars a year. And the house still costs maybe eight to twelve thousand a year to own. Try this: if you ever get a large sum, decide how much income you need first, and only then decide how much house you can afford.
scenes.caption: HOUSES COST MONEY

scenes.text: Truth number four. Where you live can double or halve what your million buys.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 4

scenes.text: Forty thousand dollars a year in a small town in the Midwest or the South is a comfortable life. The same forty thousand in San Francisco, New York City or Boston barely covers rent. Housing is the biggest expense for most households, and housing costs vary enormously between cities.
scenes.caption: SAME MONEY, DIFFERENT LIFE

scenes.text: This is why some people retire to lower cost areas, or even abroad, and suddenly their million feels like two. But moving has real costs too: leaving family, friends and a familiar doctor. Try this: look up the cost of living in two or three places you'd actually enjoy living. Compare them with where you are now. The difference might be the most powerful money move you have.
scenes.caption: CHOOSE YOUR CITY

scenes.text: Truth number five. Not every million dollars is the same, because of taxes.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 5

scenes.text: One million dollars in a traditional 401k or IRA has never been taxed. When you take money out, it's taxed as regular income. One million in a Roth account has already been taxed, so qualified withdrawals are tax free. And one million in a regular brokerage account is somewhere in between: you pay tax on the gains when you sell, often at lower long term capital gains rates.
scenes.caption: TAXES CHANGE THE NUMBER

scenes.text: So a million in a traditional account might really be worth something like eight hundred thousand to eight hundred fifty thousand after taxes, depending on your bracket. Try this: if you have retirement savings, look at which type of account they're in. Having a mix of taxable, tax deferred and tax free money gives you a lot more control later. Tax rules change, so check the current IRS limits each year.
scenes.caption: KNOW YOUR ACCOUNT TYPE

scenes.text: Truth number six. Fees can eat a huge share of your income.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 6

scenes.text: A one percent yearly advisory fee on one million dollars is ten thousand dollars a year. If your safe income is forty thousand, that fee is a quarter of it. Add fund expenses on top, and some people pay one and a half percent or more without realizing it.
scenes.caption: 1% = $10,000 A YEAR

scenes.text: That doesn't mean advice is never worth paying for. A good advisor can save you from expensive mistakes, especially with taxes and big decisions. But you should know exactly what you're paying in dollars, and what you get for it. Try this: ask for every fee in writing, as a yearly dollar amount. If someone can't give you that clearly, it tells you something.
scenes.caption: ASK IN DOLLARS

scenes.text: Truth number seven. If you stop working before sixty five, health insurance becomes a big bill.

card.title: Health insurance is the hidden bill

scenes.caption: TRUTH 7
scenes.chapter: 7. Health insurance is the hidden bill
scenes.short_hook: Before sixty five, health insurance can eat half your million dollar income.

scenes.text: Most Americans get health insurance through work. KFF's employer health benefits survey found the average total yearly premium for family coverage was close to twenty seven thousand dollars in twenty twenty five, with employers paying most of it. When you leave your job, you pay the whole thing, or buy a plan on the marketplace.
scenes.caption: THE HIDDEN BILL

scenes.text: For an early retiree living on forty thousand a year, health insurance can be one of the largest costs. Marketplace subsidies depend on your income, and the rules have changed several times. Try this: before you plan any early retirement, get a real quote for health insurance at the income you'd have. It's the number that breaks more early retirement plans than any market crash.
scenes.caption: GET A REAL QUOTE

scenes.text: Truth number eight. For most retirees, Social Security makes a million dollars go much further.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 8

scenes.text: The Social Security Administration reported that the average retired worker received around two thousand dollars a month in twenty twenty five. That's about twenty four thousand dollars a year, adjusted for inflation. For a married couple where both worked, it can be close to double.
scenes.caption: ~$2,000 A MONTH

scenes.text: So picture a retired couple with one million dollars invested. Forty thousand from the four percent rule, plus perhaps forty thousand or more from two Social Security checks. That's eighty thousand dollars a year, above what the average household spends. Try this: create an account at ssa dot gov and look at your own estimated benefit. It changes how much you really need to save.
scenes.caption: TWO INCOMES

scenes.text: Truth number nine. One million dollars at sixty five and one million at thirty five are completely different.

card.title: Early retirement is harder
card.sub: a million at 35 is not a million at 65

scenes.caption: TRUTH 9

scenes.text: At sixty five, your money needs to last maybe twenty five or thirty years. You're getting Social Security and Medicare. At thirty five, your money might need to last fifty or sixty years, with no Social Security for decades, paying for health insurance yourself, and maybe raising kids.
scenes.caption: 35 IS NOT 65

scenes.text: That's why the early retirement community often aims for twenty five to thirty three times their yearly spending, and keeps their costs low. A thirty five year old spending thirty thousand dollars a year might do it with a million. A thirty five year old spending sixty thousand would need much more. Try this: divide your investments by your yearly spending. That number, your years of freedom, is what really matters.
scenes.caption: YEARS OF FREEDOM

scenes.text: Quick pause. If these hard truths are useful, I've got videos coming on every step from zero to one million. Subscribe so you don't miss them. It's free, and it really helps the channel. Now, truth number ten.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Truth number ten. If you don't touch it, a million dollars can grow surprisingly fast.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 10

scenes.text: At a seven percent average yearly return, money roughly doubles every ten years. That's the rule of seventy two. So one million dollars left alone could become about two million in a decade. Not guaranteed, because markets go up and down, but historically, patient investors in broad markets have been rewarded over long periods.
scenes.caption: DOUBLES IN ~10 YEARS

scenes.text: This is why people who reach a million in their forties or early fifties often keep working a bit longer, even part time. A few extra years without withdrawals can change everything. Try this: if you're close to a big milestone, run the math on working two more years versus stopping now. The difference is often bigger than people expect.
scenes.caption: TWO MORE YEARS

scenes.text: Here's what that looks like. One million dollars, nothing added, at a seven percent illustration, grows to roughly two million dollars in ten years.
Truth number eleven. Your spending is the most powerful dial you have.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 11

scenes.text: Here's a quick trick from the four percent rule. Every ten thousand dollars a year you don't need to spend means you need about two hundred fifty thousand dollars less invested. Cut your yearly costs by twenty thousand, and your finish line moves half a million dollars closer.
scenes.caption: -$10K SPENDING = -$250K NEEDED

scenes.text: That's why people who reach financial independence on ordinary salaries obsess over a few big costs: housing, cars and food. Small savings help, but the big three move the number. Try this: take your yearly spending and multiply by twenty five. That's your personal number. Then see how it changes if you cut your biggest expense by ten percent.
scenes.caption: YOUR NUMBER = SPENDING x 25

scenes.text: Truth number twelve. What a million really buys is choices.

card.title: It buys choices
card.sub: the real value of a million

scenes.caption: TRUTH 12

scenes.text: Ask people who have reached a million what changed, and they rarely say stuff. They say options. They could turn down a bad job. They could take a lower paying job they love. They could take care of a parent, start a business, or take a year off without panic. The money became a kind of shield.
scenes.caption: MONEY BUYS OPTIONS

scenes.text: Even before you reach a million, you get pieces of this. One hundred thousand buys some choices. Five hundred thousand buys more. That's why the journey matters as much as the destination. Try this: write down three choices you wish you could make right now. Those are the real reasons you're saving.
scenes.caption: WRITE YOUR REASONS

scenes.text: Truth number thirteen. A million dollars can disappear faster than you think.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 13

scenes.text: Studies of athletes and sudden windfalls have found that a big pile of money doesn't automatically protect people from financial trouble. A study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research found that a significant share of former NFL players faced bankruptcy within about a dozen years of retiring, despite earning millions.
scenes.caption: WINDFALLS DISAPPEAR

scenes.text: The pattern is usually the same. Big house, several cars, generous gifts, risky investments with friends. Each one feels fine on its own. Together, they burn through seven figures. Try this: if you ever receive a large sum, park it in a safe account for six months before making any big decision. Time is the best protection against emotional spending.
scenes.caption: WAIT SIX MONTHS

scenes.text: Truth number fourteen. Most millionaires don't look like millionaires.
scenes.caption: TRUTH 14

scenes.text: UBS estimates there are more than twenty million millionaires in the United States. Most are not famous. Many are people in their fifties and sixties who owned a home for decades, saved in workplace retirement plans, and kept their spending under control. The classic book The Millionaire Next Door, by Thomas Stanley and William Danko, found the same thing back in the nineteen nineties.
scenes.caption: QUIET MILLIONAIRES

scenes.text: In other words, the people who look rich are often spending their wealth, and the people who are actually rich are often keeping it. Try this: next time you see a fancy car, remember you're seeing what someone spent, not what they have. It makes comparison a lot less powerful.
scenes.caption: SPENT VS KEPT

scenes.text: Truth number fifteen. A million dollars is more reachable than most people believe.

card.title: It's reachable
card.sub: the math of an ordinary million

scenes.caption: TRUTH 15

scenes.text: One thousand dollars a month, invested for thirty years at a seven percent average yearly return, grows to roughly one point two million dollars. You'd put in three hundred sixty thousand. The rest is growth. For a couple putting a combined fifteen percent of a hundred thousand dollar income into retirement accounts, that's not a fantasy. It's a plan.
scenes.caption: $1,000 A MONTH x 30 YEARS

scenes.text: And employer matches make it faster. If your employer matches part of your contributions, that's free money added every month. Try this: find out exactly what your workplace plan matches, and make sure you get every dollar of it. It's the easiest raise you'll ever get.
scenes.caption: GET THE FULL MATCH

scenes.text: On screen: one thousand dollars a month for thirty years at a seven percent illustration. About one point two million dollars at the end, from three hundred sixty thousand of contributions.
So what does it cost to build one million dollars by sixty five? The answer depends almost entirely on when you start. Watch how fast the price goes up.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.chapter: The price of a million at every age

scenes.text: Start at twenty five, and you have forty years. At a seven percent illustration, about three hundred eighty dollars a month gets you to one million by sixty five. That's less than many car payments.

card.note: Illustration at 7% a year, compounded monthly. Not guaranteed.

scenes.text: Wait ten years and start at thirty five, and the monthly price more than doubles, to about eight hundred twenty dollars. That's the cost of waiting a decade. Not ten percent more. More than double. Every year you wait, the mountain gets steeper, because you lose the years when compounding does its best work.
scenes.caption: THE COST OF WAITING

scenes.text: Start at forty five, with twenty years to go, and it's about nineteen hundred twenty dollars a month. Start at fifty, with fifteen years, and it's over three thousand a month.

card.note: Illustration at 7% a year, compounded monthly. Not guaranteed.

scenes.text: Now, don't let that discourage you if you're older. People in their forties and fifties usually earn more than they did at twenty five, their kids may be grown, and the mortgage may be shrinking. And employer matches and catch up contributions, which the IRS allows for people fifty and over, can carry part of the load. The point isn't that it's too late. The point is that the best day to start is always today.
scenes.caption: NEVER TOO LATE

scenes.text: And if you're young, this is the most valuable thing you'll hear all year. Three hundred eighty dollars a month, starting at twenty five, can do what three thousand a month does starting at fifty. Your biggest financial asset isn't your salary. It's your time. Spend it wisely.
scenes.caption: YOUR TIME IS YOUR ASSET

scenes.text: To make all of this real, let's meet three example people who each have exactly one million dollars. They're made up, but the math is real, and you'll probably recognize someone you know.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Three people have one million dollars. Only one of them is free.

scenes.text: Person one. Linda is sixty six and lives in a paid off house in a mid sized city in Ohio. Her one million is invested in a mix of stock and bond index funds. She withdraws about forty thousand a year, and she and her late husband's Social Security records give her around thirty thousand more. Her total costs are about fifty five thousand. Linda has a surplus every year. She travels, helps her grandkids, and never checks the market.
scenes.caption: LINDA: FREE

scenes.text: Person two. Kevin is forty one, lives in San Diego, and has one million dollars, but six hundred thousand of it is the equity in his house. He has four hundred thousand invested and a mortgage payment of four thousand dollars a month. On paper he's a millionaire. In practice, his investments could support about sixteen thousand dollars a year, and his costs are over ninety thousand. Kevin has to keep working, and he feels it.
scenes.caption: KEVIN: HOUSE RICH

scenes.text: Kevin isn't doing anything wrong. He has a valuable home and good savings. But his million is mostly locked in a place he lives, and his costs are set by an expensive city. His most powerful options are to keep investing, pay down the mortgage over time, or one day move somewhere cheaper and unlock that equity. Many millionaires on paper are in exactly his position.
scenes.caption: MILLIONAIRE ON PAPER

scenes.text: Person three. Priya is thirty four, rents a modest apartment, and has one million dollars invested across a 401k, a Roth IRA and a brokerage account. She spends thirty five thousand dollars a year. Using a more cautious three and a half percent, her investments could support about thirty five thousand a year. She's technically financially independent, at thirty four.
scenes.caption: PRIYA: INDEPENDENT AT 34

scenes.text: But Priya's money has to last fifty years or more, she pays for her own health insurance if she stops working, and she can't touch most of her retirement accounts without penalties until fifty nine and a half, except through specific IRS rules. So she chooses a middle path. She keeps working, but part time, at a job she enjoys. Her million bought her the freedom to choose.
scenes.caption: FREEDOM TO CHOOSE

scenes.text: Same number, three completely different lives. Linda is free. Kevin is house rich and cash tight. Priya has options. What made the difference wasn't the million. It was where it was held, how much they spent, and how many years it had to last. That's the whole video in three people.
scenes.caption: SAME NUMBER, 3 LIVES

scenes.text: Now the scary part. Here are five common ways a million dollars quietly disappears. Avoid these, and you're ahead of most people who ever reach seven figures.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: One. Withdrawing too much, too early. Taking eight or ten percent a year can feel fine for a while, especially in a rising market. But at that rate, a long bad stretch can drain the money in a couple of decades or less. The early years matter most, because losses then hit a bigger balance and leave less time to recover. Planners call this sequence of returns risk.
scenes.caption: 1. WITHDRAWING TOO MUCH

scenes.text: Two. Panic selling in a crash. Broad stock markets have fallen by a third or more several times in the last hundred years, and recovered every time so far, though the past is no guarantee. People who sold at the bottom locked in the loss. People who held on, or kept buying, usually came out ahead. Three. Concentration. Putting a big share into one stock, one property or one business. If it fails, you fall several levels at once.
scenes.query: Stock market chart falling on screen
scenes.caption: 2. PANIC  3. CONCENTRATION

scenes.text: Four. Lending and gifting without limits. When people learn you have money, requests arrive. Family, friends, business ideas. Helping people you love can be wonderful, but set a yearly amount you can give without hurting your own plan, and stick to it. A no today can protect your ability to say yes for decades.
scenes.caption: 4. LENDING WITHOUT LIMITS

scenes.text: Five. Scams and too good to be true investments. Fake crypto platforms, romance scams, guaranteed returns, urgent calls pretending to be your bank. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center reports billions of dollars in losses every year, and older Americans report some of the largest losses. If anyone pressures you to act fast, or promises high returns with no risk, stop and hang up.
scenes.caption: 5. SCAMS

scenes.text: Angle two. The psychology. Because the strangest thing about one million dollars is how it feels when you actually get there.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Why does a million dollars feel like less than you expected?

scenes.text: Many people expect reaching a million to feel like crossing a finish line. Fireworks. Relief. Instead, a lot of people say it feels oddly normal. They check the number, smile, and go back to work the next day. Psychologists call this hedonic adaptation. We get used to new situations quickly, good and bad. The thrill fades, and the new level becomes the baseline.
scenes.caption: IT FEELS NORMAL

scenes.text: That's why the million should never be the goal on its own. If it's just a number, it disappoints. If it's connected to something you want, like time with your kids, a business, or leaving a job you hate, then hitting it means something. The number is just a vehicle. The destination is the life it buys.
scenes.caption: A VEHICLE, NOT A DESTINATION

scenes.text: There's another trap called moving the goalposts. At five hundred thousand, people say they'll feel safe at a million. At a million, they say two million. The Schwab survey we mentioned shows the same thing at the level of the whole country. The definition of wealthy keeps rising. Without a clear personal number, enough never arrives.
scenes.caption: MOVING THE GOALPOSTS

scenes.text: The opposite also happens. Some people feel a million is so far away that they never start. It seems impossible, so why bother? This is where the math is your friend. Nobody saves a million dollars. They save a few hundred dollars, over and over, and let time do the heavy lifting. Break it down, and the mountain becomes a staircase.
scenes.caption: A MOUNTAIN OR A STAIRCASE

scenes.text: And finally, there's fear of spending. People who spent decades saving often find it painful to withdraw, even when they can clearly afford it. Research on retirees has found many spend less than they safely could. If that's you someday, remember that the money was always meant to be used. Saved money that's never enjoyed is a kind of failure too.
scenes.caption: LET YOURSELF SPEND

scenes.text: So the psychological lesson of a million dollars is simple. Define enough before you get there. Connect the money to a purpose. And give yourself permission to enjoy it when the time comes. People who do those three things tend to be much happier with their money, whatever the final number is.
scenes.caption: DEFINE ENOUGH

scenes.text: Angle three. The playbook. If you have a million dollars, or you're on your way, here's how to make it actually work for you.
scenes.caption: RYAN
scenes.short_hook: Here's how to make one million dollars last for the rest of your life.

scenes.text: Step one. Know your number. Add up what you spend in a year, not what you think you spend, what you actually spend. Look at a full year of bank and card statements. Multiply by twenty five for a traditional retirement, or by about thirty if you want extra safety or plan to retire early. That's your target, and it might be more or less than a million.
scenes.caption: STEP 1: KNOW YOUR NUMBER

scenes.text: Step two. Keep it diversified and low cost. Many long term investors use broad index funds that hold thousands of companies, plus some bonds as they get closer to needing the money. You don't need to pick winners. You need to own the market cheaply and stay invested. Check your fees once a year.
scenes.query: New York Stock Exchange trading floor
scenes.caption: STEP 2: LOW COST, DIVERSIFIED

scenes.text: Step three. Keep a cash buffer. Many retirees keep one to two years of spending in cash or very safe investments. When markets fall, they spend from the buffer instead of selling investments at low prices. It's one of the simplest ways to make the four percent rule safer.
scenes.caption: STEP 3: A CASH BUFFER

scenes.text: Step four. Be flexible. The people whose money lasts the longest usually spend a little less in bad years and a little more in good years. Skipping one big trip during a downturn can make a real difference over thirty years. Step five. Plan your taxes. Decide which accounts to draw from first. A tax professional can be worth the fee here, especially in the first years.
scenes.caption: STEPS 4 AND 5

scenes.text: Step six. Protect it. Make sure you have the right insurance, a will, and beneficiaries named on every account. Be extremely careful with anyone who promises guaranteed high returns. The Federal Reserve found that about one in five adults experienced fraud or a scam in a single year. People with money are bigger targets, not smaller ones.
scenes.caption: STEP 6: PROTECT IT

scenes.text: And if you're still on your way to a million, the playbook is even simpler. Spend less than you earn. Invest the difference automatically in low cost, diversified funds. Get every dollar of employer match. Avoid high interest debt. And don't interrupt the process. That's genuinely most of it.
scenes.caption: THE ROAD TO A MILLION

scenes.text: Let me answer the questions people ask me most about a million dollars.
scenes.caption: RYAN

scenes.text: Question one. Is a million enough to retire? For many people, combined with Social Security and a paid off home, yes. For people in very expensive cities, or retiring very young, maybe not. It comes back to your spending. Question two. Should I pay off my house first? It's a personal choice. A paid off house lowers the income you need, but it ties up money you can't easily spend.
scenes.caption: IS IT ENOUGH?

scenes.text: Question three. What if I inherit a million? Slow down. Put it somewhere safe and boring, pay off high interest debt, and talk to a fee only financial planner before doing anything big. Question four. Can I live off interest alone? If safe bonds pay around four percent, one million earns around forty thousand a year, before taxes, without touching the principal. But interest rates change, and inflation slowly eats away at a fixed income.
scenes.caption: INHERITANCE AND INTEREST

scenes.text: Question five. How long does it take to save a million? It depends almost entirely on how much you invest each month. At a seven percent illustration, two thousand dollars a month gets there in about twenty years. One thousand a month takes around twenty eight. Five hundred a month takes around thirty six. Start earlier, and time does more of the work.
scenes.caption: HOW LONG DOES IT TAKE?

scenes.text: Question six. Does a million make you happy? Research on income and happiness, including well known work by Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton, and later work by Matthew Killingsworth, suggests money is linked to well being, especially in removing stress. But the biggest gains come from escaping money worries, not from luxury. A million dollars can buy you calm. It can't buy you purpose. You have to bring that yourself.
scenes.caption: DOES IT MAKE YOU HAPPY?

scenes.text: Question seven. Should I tell people I have a million? Many quiet millionaires don't. Not out of secrecy, but because it changes how people treat you, and it makes you a target for sales pitches and scams. Share it with your partner, your planner and the people who need to know for your estate. Beyond that, your net worth is your business. Question eight. Is a million still worth chasing? Absolutely. Just know what you're chasing: not a rich lifestyle, but a life where money stops making your decisions for you.
scenes.caption: KEEP IT QUIET?

scenes.text: Let's recap the fifteen truths. One, inflation has cut the million in half since the nineties. Two, as an income it's about forty thousand dollars a year. Three, a house alone would eat it. Four, location changes everything. Five, taxes take a slice. Six, fees can eat a quarter of your income. Seven, health insurance is the hidden bill before sixty five. Eight, Social Security helps a lot.
scenes.caption: TRUTHS 1 TO 8

scenes.text: Nine, early retirement is much harder. Ten, investing makes it grow. Eleven, spending is the real dial. Twelve, it buys choices. Thirteen, lifestyle can burn it fast. Fourteen, most millionaires look ordinary. And fifteen, a million is more reachable than most people believe, with time and consistency.
scenes.caption: TRUTHS 9 TO 15

scenes.text: And the three angles. The numbers say a million is comfortable, not rich, and your spending decides how far it goes. The psychology says define enough before you get there. And the playbook says keep it simple, low cost, diversified, protected, and flexible.
scenes.caption: NUMBERS, PSYCHOLOGY, PLAYBOOK

scenes.text: And one last thought before you go. When people picture a million dollars, they picture a pile of cash, and what they could buy with it. But the people who handle money best picture something else. They picture a machine, quietly producing income month after month, year after year, so that their time belongs to them. A pile of cash gets spent. A machine keeps working. Whether your million becomes a pile or a machine is the most important money decision you'll ever make, and it's a decision you can start making today, long before you reach seven figures.
scenes.caption: A PILE OR A MACHINE?

scenes.text: So here's your homework. Work out your own number: your yearly spending times twenty five. Then compare it with a million. You might find your finish line is closer than you thought. Or you might find it's further away, and that's useful too, because now you know exactly what you're aiming at. Either way, write the number down somewhere you'll see it every month. If you want the full step by step plan, it's in my playbook, link in the description. I'm Ryan Rover. See you in the next one.
scenes.caption: RYAN
